species.shortDescription: A tropical climbing evergreen native to the rainforests of southern Mexico and Central America, grown worldwide as a houseplant.
species.origin: Native to the tropical rainforests of southern Mexico and Central America, where it climbs tree trunks using aerial roots and can reach 20 m in height.
curiosities: The name deliciosa refers to its edible fruit, which tastes like a blend of pineapple and banana when fully ripe.
Leaf holes, called fenestrations, are thought to help the plant withstand strong winds and let light reach lower leaves.
Unripe fruit contains oxalic acid and is an irritant, so it must be eaten only when fully mature.
species.toxicity: Leaves and unripe fruit are toxic to cats and dogs and irritating to humans (calcium oxalate crystals).

species.shortDescription: A hardy evergreen vine from the arum family, one of the most popular and forgiving houseplants.
species.origin: Native to Mo'orea in the Society Islands of French Polynesia; now naturalised across tropical forests worldwide.
curiosities: Called 'devil's ivy' because it is nearly impossible to kill and stays green even in low light.
In the wild its leaves can grow over a metre long, but indoors they usually stay palm-sized.
It rarely flowers in cultivation — the last recorded spontaneous bloom was in 1964.
species.toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and humans if chewed or swallowed (insoluble calcium oxalates).

species.shortDescription: A West African fig with large, violin-shaped leathery leaves, popular as a statement indoor tree.
species.origin: Native to lowland tropical rainforest in western Africa, from Cameroon west to Sierra Leone.
curiosities: The species name lyrata and the common name both refer to the lyre- or fiddle-shaped leaves.
In the wild it often begins life as an epiphyte on another tree, then sends roots down and can strangle its host.
It resents being moved and may drop leaves after a change in light or location.
species.toxicity: Sap is mildly toxic and can irritate skin and the mouth of pets and humans.

species.shortDescription: A stiff-leaved evergreen succulent from West Africa, extremely drought-tolerant and low-light tolerant.
species.origin: Native to tropical West Africa, from Nigeria east to the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
curiosities: Formerly classified as Sansevieria trifasciata; moved to Dracaena on genetic evidence in 2017.
It performs CAM photosynthesis, opening its pores at night, so it keeps releasing oxygen after dark.
Its leaf fibres, called bowstring hemp, have traditionally been used to make rope and baskets.
species.toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs (saponins); can cause nausea and drooling if eaten.

species.shortDescription: A short-stemmed succulent with thick, gel-filled leaves, cultivated for millennia for its soothing gel.
species.origin: Origin uncertain; likely the Arabian Peninsula, now cultivated and naturalised across arid regions worldwide.
curiosities: The leaf gel is about 99% water; the rest is a mix of vitamins, enzymes and polysaccharides.
It has been used medicinally for over 6,000 years — depictions appear in ancient Egyptian carvings.
The yellow latex just under the skin is a strong laxative and quite bitter, unlike the clear inner gel.
species.toxicity: The leaf latex is toxic to cats, dogs and humans if ingested; the clear inner gel is generally safe.
